parts.title: Registering with a doctor's surgery
parts.context: A man phones a doctor's surgery to register as a new patient.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 1. You will hear a man telephoning a doctor's surgery to register as a new patient. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: You will see that there is an example that has been done for you. On this occasion only, the conversation relating to this will be played first.

script.speaker: julia
script.text: Kestrel Lane Surgery, good morning. Julia speaking.

script.speaker: neil
script.text: Oh, good morning. I wonder if you can help me. I've just moved house, and I need to find a new doctor. Is it possible to register over the phone?

script.speaker: julia
script.text: Yes, it is. It only takes a few minutes, and I'll fill in the form as we go along.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: The man has just moved house, so 'moved house' has been written in the space. Now we shall begin. You should answer the questions as you listen, because you will not hear the recording a second time. Listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: julia
script.text: Right, could I have your full name, please?

script.speaker: neil
script.text: Yes, it's Neil Hargreaves.

script.speaker: julia
script.text: Sorry, could you spell your surname for me?

script.speaker: neil
script.text: Of course. That's H-A-R-G-R-E-A-V-E-S.

script.speaker: julia
script.text: Thank you. And what's your new address?

script.speaker: neil
script.text: It's forty-three Cedar Road.

script.speaker: julia
script.text: Cedar Road. Is that the new estate behind the garden centre?

script.speaker: neil
script.text: That's the one. The houses are so new that you might not find them on the map yet. We only moved in at the weekend.

script.speaker: julia
script.text: That's all right. And your date of birth?

script.speaker: neil
script.text: The fourteenth of March. Oh, no, sorry, that's my wife's birthday. Mine's the twenty-fourth. I always get the two of them mixed up.

script.speaker: julia
script.text: Not to worry. The twenty-fourth of March. And what do you do for a living? We ask for your occupation.

script.speaker: neil
script.text: Well, I started out as a carpenter, but these days I'm an architect. I work for a firm in the city centre.

script.speaker: julia
script.text: Lovely. And which surgery were you with before?

script.speaker: neil
script.text: It was the Riverside Health Centre, in Dunmore.

script.speaker: julia
script.text: Riverside. Right, thank you. I'll ask them to send your records over. It usually takes about a week.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: julia
script.text: And how long were you registered at the Riverside?

script.speaker: neil
script.text: Eight years. I lived in Dunmore for twelve altogether, but I didn't join the Riverside until my daughter was born.

script.speaker: julia
script.text: I see. Now, do you have any allergies we should know about?

script.speaker: neil
script.text: Penicillin. It gives me a terrible rash. I used to think I was allergic to shellfish as well, but I had some tests last year, and it turns out I'm not.

script.speaker: julia
script.text: That's good news. I'll just put penicillin, then. Now, when you come in, we need to see some documents. First, photo ID, so a passport or a driving licence will do. And we also need proof of your new address. We used to accept a gas or electricity bill, but we've stopped doing that. These days it has to be a recent bank statement.

script.speaker: neil
script.text: That's no problem. I've got one from last month.

script.speaker: julia
script.text: Perfect. Finally, we like all new patients to have a health check with our practice nurse. I can offer you Tuesday at ten o'clock.

script.speaker: neil
script.text: Oh, I can't do Tuesdays, I'm afraid. I'm on building sites all day. Have you got anything on Thursday?

script.speaker: julia
script.text: Let me look. Um, yes, Thursday at ten is free.

script.speaker: neil
script.text: That's perfect. Put me down for that, please.

script.speaker: julia
script.text: Right. Oh, hold on, I'm so sorry. I've just noticed that the nurse is away on a training course on Thursday. I could offer you Friday instead.

script.speaker: neil
script.text: Friday's fine.

script.speaker: julia
script.text: Although I'm afraid the only appointment she has left is at nine o'clock.

script.speaker: neil
script.text: That's all right. I can go to work afterwards.

script.speaker: julia
script.text: Lovely. So that's Friday at nine. We'll send you a reminder by text message, and a letter confirming your registration should arrive next week. Thank you for registering with us, Mr Hargreaves.

script.speaker: neil
script.text: Thank you very much. Goodbye.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 1. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: A town book fair
parts.context: The organiser of a town's annual book fair briefs a group of volunteers.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 2. You will hear the organiser of a town's annual book fair talking to a group of volunteers. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: fiona
script.text: Good evening, everyone, and thank you for coming. I'm Fiona Garrick, and I chair the committee that organises the Marlbury Book Fair. This is our twentieth year, and we're going to need every one of you.

script.speaker: fiona
script.text: Several of you have asked how it all began. A lot of people assume it was the library's idea, since the library is such a big part of it now. But in fact it started much more modestly. A bookseller called Mr Okoro, who had a shop on Bridge Street, had a cellar crammed with books that nobody had bought, and he couldn't face throwing them away. So one Saturday he put them out on tables in the market square, and invited a few friends to do the same. It was only meant to happen once, but hundreds of people turned up. The schools joined in later, but that came afterwards.

script.speaker: fiona
script.text: So, what's new this year? We did think about adding a Friday, so that the fair would run for three days, but you would all be exhausted, so it stays at two. Entry will be free again, because that's what makes the fair special. No, the real change is that, for the first time, we've invited writers from the area to enter a short-story competition.

script.speaker: fiona
script.text: People often ask about money. We don't charge visitors, so where does it come from? The council gave us a grant in the early years, but that ended a long time ago. These days, the people who rent tables pay a small fee, which covers our printing and insurance, but the bulk of our income comes from local firms. The bakery and the bank each sponsor an event, and without them we simply couldn't do it.

script.speaker: fiona
script.text: Now, every year something goes wrong, and this year it's books. Not a shortage, quite the opposite. Once word got out that we were collecting, people brought in so many boxes that we've run out of places to put them. The library storeroom has been full since February, and we're using the vestry at St Mark's as well. As for volunteers, forty of you is a record. And yes, one of our authors had to cancel because of illness, but we found a replacement within a day.
script.tts: Now, every year something goes wrong, and this year it's books. Not a shortage, quite the opposite. Once word got out that we were collecting, people brought in so many boxes that we've run out of places to put them. The library storeroom has been full since February, and we're using the vestry at Saint Mark's as well. As for volunteers, forty of you is a record. And yes, one of our authors had to cancel because of illness, but we found a replacement within a day.

script.speaker: fiona
script.text: So, what do I need from you? Many of you have already told me which day you prefer, but I still need to know which hours you're free, so please fill in the green form at the back of the room before you leave tonight. There's no training session, I'm pleased to say, and I'll decide which event each of you helps at, so please don't ask for particular ones.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: fiona
script.text: Right, now the programme. The main sale is in the Corn Exchange on both days from ten o'clock. But there are also five special events, and some things have changed since the leaflet was printed, so please listen carefully.

script.speaker: fiona
script.text: First, the poetry evening on Saturday night. The leaflet says it's in St Mark's church hall, but, as I said, that's now full of boxes, so it has moved to the Regal, which used to be the town's cinema until the nineties. It's a better venue anyway.
script.tts: First, the poetry evening on Saturday night. The leaflet says it's in Saint Mark's church hall, but, as I said, that's now full of boxes, so it has moved to the Regal, which used to be the town's cinema until the nineties. It's a better venue anyway.

script.speaker: fiona
script.text: On Sunday morning there'll be stories for the under-fives. Last year they were at the museum, but the museum is being redecorated, so this year it's in the children's section of the library.

script.speaker: fiona
script.text: Then comes the main attraction, the interviews with visiting authors. We thought about putting those in the Corn Exchange, but with the sale going on, it would be far too noisy. So they're upstairs in the Town Hall, in the council chamber.

script.speaker: fiona
script.text: On Saturday afternoon, you can learn to bind your own notebook. It needs a large table and a sink for the glue, which is why we're using the education room at the museum.

script.speaker: fiona
script.text: And finally, on Sunday afternoon, there's the book swap. You bring a book you've finished with, and take away one you haven't read. This will be out in the market square, where the first fair was held, though if it rains we'll have to move everyone into the Corn Exchange.

script.speaker: fiona
script.text: That's the programme. Please fill in the green form before you go. Thank you all very much.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 2. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: A model-bridge project
parts.context: Two engineering students discuss a model-bridge project with their tutor.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 3. You will hear two engineering students, Ellie and Marcus, discussing a model-bridge project with their tutor, Dr Whitaker. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: whitaker
script.text: Come in, both of you. Let's see where you've got to with the bridge. When we last spoke, you were still deciding on the design.

script.speaker: marcus
script.text: We were. I'll be honest, Dr Whitaker, I really wanted to build an arch. They look so elegant.

script.speaker: ellie
script.text: But it wouldn't have worked, would it? An arch pushes outwards at the bottom, and the test rig only has two plain supports, with nothing to stop the ends sliding apart.

script.speaker: marcus
script.text: True. And it wasn't the weight, because arches can be really light, and I'm sure we could have cut the pieces accurately enough. It was just the supports. So we've gone for a truss.

script.speaker: whitaker
script.text: Sensible. Now, you made a prototype, I gather. How did it go?

script.speaker: ellie
script.text: Well, we loaded it in the workshop on Friday. It held about nine kilos, and then it suddenly collapsed.

script.speaker: marcus
script.text: We assumed the wood had snapped. We'd chosen quite thin sticks to keep the weight down. It did bend a lot before it went, too, but that's just what balsa does. Anyway, when we looked at the pieces, none of the beams was actually broken. It was the joints. The glue had simply let go.

script.speaker: marcus
script.text: So we thought, more glue at every joint.

script.speaker: whitaker
script.text: I'd resist that. Extra glue adds weight, and a big blob of dried glue is quite brittle. What I'd do instead is look up gusset plates. They're just little triangles of thin card, which you glue over each joint so that the load spreads out. They weigh almost nothing, and make a huge difference.

script.speaker: ellie
script.text: Good idea. We were also wondering about thicker sticks for the diagonals.

script.speaker: whitaker
script.text: You could, but you'd lose out on the weight side of the marking. Try the plates first.

script.speaker: ellie
script.text: How does the marking work, exactly? Is it simply whoever's bridge holds the most?

script.speaker: whitaker
script.text: No, and that's where some groups come unstuck. The first part is the load your bridge carries before it fails, but that's judged against its own weight, so a very light bridge that holds a lot scores higher than a heavy one that holds a little more. The second part is a prediction. Before the test, you hand in your estimate of the breaking load, and the closer you are, the more marks you get.

script.speaker: marcus
script.text: So it doesn't matter what it looks like?

script.speaker: whitaker
script.text: Not in the slightest. Nor does how fast you build it. You've all been given the same wood, so cost doesn't come into it either.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: whitaker
script.text: Right, now your list of materials for the final bridge, because anything special has to be ordered by Friday. Balsa first.

script.speaker: ellie
script.text: Yes, we're using it for the main frame again.

script.speaker: whitaker
script.text: Fine, but a word of warning. Balsa is beautifully light, but no two sticks are the same. Even in one packet, some are twice as stiff as others. So test each one by flexing it, and save the stiffest for the parts that carry the most load.

script.speaker: marcus
script.text: OK, we hadn't thought of that. We've also got some bamboo skewers for the diagonals. They're incredibly strong for their weight.

script.speaker: whitaker
script.text: They are, I'll give you that. The trouble is attaching them. They're thin, round and slippery, so glue just won't hold them firmly in place.

script.speaker: ellie
script.text: Right. And for the glue itself, we've been using ordinary white wood glue.

script.speaker: whitaker
script.text: Fine. You might be tempted by epoxy, which is stronger, but you can only buy it from one supplier in town, and it's a nuisance to mix. So stay with the white glue, but allow plenty of time, because it takes ages to dry properly.

script.speaker: marcus
script.text: Could we use a bit of sticky tape to hold things together while the glue sets?

script.speaker: whitaker
script.text: I'm afraid not. The rules are quite clear. It's wood, card and glue, and nothing else. Even a tiny strip of tape, and you're disqualified.

script.speaker: ellie
script.text: And what about a coat of varnish, to protect it?

script.speaker: whitaker
script.text: It would look nice, but varnish is heavy, and it does nothing at all for the strength. You'd be penalised for the extra weight and get nothing back.

script.speaker: marcus
script.text: OK. We'll finalise the list tonight.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 3. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Lecture: the migration of Arctic terns
parts.context: A lecture about the long-distance migration of Arctic terns.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 4. You will hear a lecture about the migration of Arctic terns. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Good morning, everyone. Today I want to talk about a seabird that holds a world record: the Arctic tern. It's a slender, elegant bird, white and pale grey, with a black cap and a bright red beak, and it weighs about as much as a bar of soap. Yet it makes the longest migration of any animal on the planet. It breeds in the far north, in places like Greenland and Iceland, and it spends our winter in the far south, around the edge of Antarctica. And it makes that round trip every single year.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: So why go to all that trouble? Well, the simple answer is food. The terns eat mostly small fish, although they'll take insects too. Their hunting method is hovering above the water, perfectly still, and then plunging in headfirst when they spot a fish. In the Arctic summer, with the sun hardly setting, the seas are full of fish. But when that summer ends, the fish move away, and the birds simply follow the summer south. So a tern lives through two summers every year, and probably sees more daylight than any other creature on Earth.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: For most of the twentieth century, we knew surprisingly little about how they made the journey. Scientists fitted numbered metal rings to the legs of chicks, and then waited for somebody to find the bird, usually dead, and report the number. That told us where a bird began and where it ended up, but nothing about the route in between. Radio transmitters might have helped, but even the smallest ones were far too heavy for a bird this size.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The breakthrough came about fifteen years ago, with a device called a geolocator. It weighs about a gram, and it's attached to the bird's leg ring. Now, it doesn't use satellites. And, sorry, I see my slide says it records temperature, but that's a mistake. What it actually records is the level of light, every few minutes. From the times of sunrise and sunset, researchers can work out where the bird was on any given day. The weakness is that a geolocator can't send out its information; it can only store it. So the data can't be collected unless the same bird is caught again, a year later, which is a lot harder than it sounds.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: So, what did the data show? Well, it overturned a few assumptions. You'd expect the birds to fly in a straight line down the Atlantic, but they don't. They follow an enormous S-shaped route. You might guess they're following ocean currents, but the tracking showed that it's the winds that matter. The terns choose the route where the prevailing winds are behind them, so although the zigzag makes the journey longer, it's faster, and uses less energy, than battling into a headwind. Over a year, a tern flies around seventy thousand kilometres.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Another surprise was that the birds don't fly non-stop. On the way south, there's a long stopover in the middle of the North Atlantic, where they stay for about a month. Food is plentiful there, so the terns feed heavily, building up reserves of fat for the long flight ahead. After that, they head down the coast of West Africa, and reach the edge of the Antarctic ice, usually in December. They stay through the southern summer, and fly back north, arriving at their breeding colonies in May.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Now, the breeding colonies. Arctic terns nest on open ground, usually on gravel or sand, and they make little more than a shallow hollow. That leaves the eggs and chicks very exposed, to foxes, to gulls, and even to people walking past. So the terns have developed a ferocious defence. They treat anything that wanders into the colony as an intruder, and they dive at it, striking it on the head with their beaks.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Finally, the future. Arctic terns can live for thirty years, which adds up to the equivalent of three trips to the Moon and back. But the species is under pressure. In some regions, the numbers of sandeels, the small fish that terns feed their chicks on, have fallen sharply. Overfishing has played a part in some places, but the main cause is climate change, because the ocean is getting warmer. Where the fish decline, chicks starve.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: That's all for today. Next week, we'll look at how young birds find their way.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 4. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of the Listening test.
